Hi @davidpanderson,

Maybe I should be a bit more detailed since you may not be aware of the components of this solution. The idle_detect component IS the analogue of the BOINC tray for Linux. It is started when the user logs in using systemd's user level service architecture. It's job, similar to BOINC tray, is to collect idle information from the user session context, i.e. the Window manager (X/Wayland compositor).

There is a separate component, event_detect, run as a system service and I would like to go through and explain the rationale for that. Unlike Windows, Linux does not allow access to pointer devices directly unless the user is a member of the input group. It is not desirable nor necessary to give the logged in normal user access to the input devices via adding them to the input group, because that would be read/write, as the input device modes are 660 and it is not a good idea to change the mode via udev as there may be unintended consequences or security issues generated. However, we need to be able to capture input device activity directly as a fallback, because of the fractured nature of the Window manager environment on Linux (unlike Windows which is completely standardized). Running a separate, very small system service, event_detect, in a sandbox with access to scan the input devices and the pts/ttys for terminal activity solves that problem.

On the X side, things are pretty standardized (except the ability to suspend the idle - idle inhibit - when the user is watching a movie), but on the Wayland side things are far more fractured. Currently idle_detect (the user component) handles KDE and Gnome with both X and Wayland WITH idle inhibit functionality, but non Gnome, non KDE X will degrade to XSS access, which doesn't take into account idle inhibit, and finally the corner case which makes event_detect important, non Gnome, non KDE Wayland. For those, there is no standard approach to interfacing with the compositor that reliably detects idleness nor idle inhibit. For this the user component falls back to raw pointing device activity though event_detect.

Why have the boinc client pointed to the event detect service rather than directly to the idle_detect user component? There are several good reasons.

1. Linux is multi-user. There very well could be more than one X session, in addition to many non GUI logins. Conversely the person could log off the main console and there may be NO GUI session at all besides the SDDM login manager. (See #2199 and #2535, for example.) Unlike Windows, the normal mode for the boinc client is to run as a system service under the boinc user account, in a sandbox of sorts. This means that having the boinc client connect to the idle_detect instance directly would be complicated and error prone as it would have to deal with the coming and going of every idle_detect instance directly.
2. It is better for the boinc-client to communicate with a small system level service in a sandbox security-wise than directly with the user level idle_detect instances. The user level idle_detect instance(s) (note the plural there) forward their idle information efficiently to the system-level service via a very small message, of which is validated upon receipt. The system level event_detect service then combines that into an overall idle picture. Note this is a PUSH from the user level idle_detect service(s) rather than pull, which means that the architecture deals efficiently with 0 to n instances of the user level idle_detect instances. The system service then provides the overall last_active_time.dat which is readable by any DC system that needs accurate idle detection.
3. This drastically simplifies the logic in the boinc-client itself. It does not need to worry about the presence or number of user logins/instances. It simply pulls the last_active_time.dat from a file, which is consistent and present for the entire duration of the machine uptime.

Note that this file, which is in /run/event_detect is in memory only. If you prefer, we can use mmap to make it a truly memory mapped file. Mmap is much preferred over the older shmem.

According to my data, the average ratio of int speed to FP speed is about 4.
So if you have an app that does N integer ops and no floating point,
use rsc_fpops_est = N/4,
and similar for rsc_fpops_bound

The only headers that should be getting installed are the interfaces
for the API and library.
Implementation stuff like str_replace.h should not be installed.

opencl_boinc.h includes parse.h, which includes str_util.h, which includes str_replace.h . So in order to use an installed opencl_boinc.h, str_replace.h needs to be installed as well.

So it's some other header in that chain that needs to be fixed.
Once that is done, please review and partially revert #6240.

I keep this open for a while to make a full test with building `libboinc` independently and linking to the test code.
Should take me a couple of days to do that.

BTW, the test is: compile an app that uses libboinc_api and libboinc
(and therefore includes api/boinc_api.h and e.g. lib/util.h)
without config.h anywhere.
I did this using samples/example_app/ (by renaming boinc/config.h)
on Win and Linux and it worked.

That's similar to what I plan to do, with the only different that in my case I want to have these builds separated, and the app should not have physical access to the 'config.h' file to be sure that there is no other hidden place.

app versions that use a GPU.
This by definition can't be zero.

This PR is Redundant. The Xcode project builds a utility _SetVersion_ from _ClientGUI/Mac/Setversion.cpp_ which updates the version numbers in all 12 plist files, based on the value of `BOINC_VERSION_STRING` in _version.h_. This has been present for many years.

> The Xcode project builds a utility SetVersion 

... and runs it every time it builds BOINC. This guarantees that all the components of BOINC always have the same version number as provided by _version.h_, automatically.
Of course it can be zero if the graphics card isn't used.  Zero is also the default boinc itself puts in if the line is omitted!

> The <gpu_usage> specifies the (possibly fractional) GPU usage for app versions that use a GPU. This by definition can't be zero.

By definition all PCs use a CPU.  It then follows that the CPU cannot be 0 and the test for non-negative CPU is coded incorrectly ;)

## Goals

A project (e.g. BOINC Central) may have jobs with various science areas and locations.
Volunteers should be able to use keyword prefs to control what jobs they get.

This currently works if the volunteer uses Science United.
It should also work if they're attached to the project directly.
This means letting them edit keyword prefs on the project web site.

## Terms

* A 'full keyword' is ID, name, category, parent
* A 'keyword ID' is just the ID (int)
* A 'user KW prefs' is lists of yes and no KW IDs

## Current:

Account manager RPC:
* reply includes user KW prefs.
These are stored in the acct_mgr_login.xml file, and in the ACCT_MGR_INFO object in memory.

Scheduler RPC:
* request: includes user KW prefs (from acct mgr)
* replies: workunits have "job_keyword_ids": lists of IDs

Client:
* reads list of all full keywords from a file 'keywords.xml'.
I'm not sure where this file comes from; it's not updated by the client.

GUI RPC:
* replies: workunits have list of full keywords

Job submission:
* create_work has a --keywords arg (list of IDs).
This should get stored in workunit.keywords (check that it does this, and that they're added to xml_doc when job is sent).

## Design decisions

* Do we want keywords.xml on clients?
    * No; keep it simple

* Should KW prefs propagate between projects, like computing prefs?
    * No; keep it simple

* where to store per-user KW prefs on server?
    * for now, in text files (not DB)

## Changes

client/manager:
* don't include job keywords in GUI RPC
* don't show user or job keywords anywhere;
user can see job keywords on project web site if they want

Is the real question here “Why are BOINC’s remaining-time estimates so wrong when apps are supplying reliable progress information?”
Similar: #4880

The answer is the stupid way Boinc calculates times.  Every time you get a task you haven't done some of before, it guesses how long it will take.  Say it guesses 10 hours, but it's really going to take 1 hour.  It does 10% in 6 minutes.  Boinc still thinks the other 90% will take 90% of it's 10 hour estimate, so 9 hours.  Insanity.  Fraction done exact is the only sensible way to calculate times.  The guess should only be used for unstarted tasks.  I can't think of a single project which doesn't provide accurate progress.  There can't be many at all.  Anyway, if it didn't, the current method is still no good!

Like much of BOINC: it’s complicated (starting from the core assumption that parts of the ecosystem are unreliable), and will have grown over the years to cope with a wide variety of project requirements and application behaviours.

The current calculation puts a lot of faith in the projects’ own estimates of workunit size, so the client can’t be blamed for those being inaccurate.

Perhaps the algorithm could be made adaptive: keeping track of different estimates over time, it could learn which method is the most suitable for each app. But that’s a lot easier said than done…

What is accurate (for 95%+ of projects) is the percentage done.  So just use fraction done exact all the time.  The project estimate doesn't evaluate how fast your processor core or GPU is very well.  You would think it would use the flops from the Boinc CPU test, so I don't know why it's so terrible, but it is.

I suspect most of the current behaviour is a legacy of the early days: CPU speeds were more predictable, GPUs weren’t a thing, projects were good at calculating the size of their workunits, and apps were bad at reporting progress.

Now, as you point out, few of those things are true. Maybe it is appropriate to rethink the time calculation wholesale.

FWIW I “+1” this feature request, as I also find myself setting `fraction_done_exact` everywhere – but I only run a couple of projects, so I’ve no idea what the rest of the BOINC world looks like.

After careful consideration, it was decided not to continue this piece of functionality.
There are several reasons for that.

1. Even having BOINC client running inside browser doesn't mean that there will be any projects interested in porting their applications to WASM (as an example, we have for years the support of GPU applications on Android, but there was never any application ported to it; the same situation is with Windows on ARM: BOINC client has this support for a couple of years already, but no projects that could run on it).
2. Applications that run in browser don't have direct access to the hard disk the same way native applications do. IN order to do that we need to support [FileSystemAPI](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/FileSystemDirectoryEntry). But then the science application should have this support too.
3. Even when claimed that WASM applications have almost the same performance as the native applications, our first internal tests showed that the WASM application is much slower than the native one.

Considering all this, we don't see that there is any reason to spend time and resources on building the functionality that will never be used.
We can come back to this again if something significant happens in the world (e.g. huge amount of devices will appear on market that can run browser applications only (no, this is not the case of [ChomeBooks](https://support.google.com/chromebook/answer/7021273?hl=en#zippy=)).

For this reason, we are closing this feature request, and all the test functionality that was added for WASM will be removed during the next few days to keep our repo as clean as possible (I know, there is still a huge work need to be done to prettify the repo, but that's my goal for the couple of next iterations).

My understanding of the system- the initial Remaining (estimated) time is set by the project- the Scheduler uses the estimated FLOPS of the Task and the reported FLOPS of the compute device it is allocated to, to estimate the likely processing time- which is the Remaining (estimated) time displayed in the BOINC client.

From memory, after 10 Tasks are returned and verified, from then on the Runtimes of completed Tasks are then used to refine the Remaining (estimated) time.

As returned Tasks are reported, and when new Tasks are allocated, the Remaining (estimated) time on the client is updated using the previously returned Task Runtimes.

So it would appear it is sending the actual Runtimes for the completed Tasks to the server.

To let BOINC use all GPUs installed, you need to add to the `cc_config.xml` file this option:
```
<use_all_gpus>0|1</use_all_gpus>
```
To tell BOINC to ignore any particular GPU, you need to add to the `cc_config.xml` file this option:
```
<exclude_gpu>
    <url>project_URL</url>
    [<device_num>N</device_num>]
    [<type>NVIDIA|ATI|intel_gpu</type>]
    [<app>appname</app>]
</exclude_gpu>
```

Use this wiki page for the detailed explanation of these (and other) options: https://github.com/BOINC/boinc/wiki/Client-configuration

Ok, let's assume, you know in advance, how much time any particular inpot data will take to finish the calculation.
Then create the next plan classes:

For what it's worth the underlying bug is real and small if a maintainer wants to take it independently: in lib/str_util.cpp, lf_terminate() evaluates `p[n-1]` with n = strlen(p); for an empty string (n==0) that reads p[-1] out of bounds. read_file_malloc() returns a valid empty buffer for a 0-byte file, so e.g. an empty gui_urls.xml reaches it via GUI_URLS::init(). Guarding with `n>0` fixes it. Thanks for maintaining BOINC.

The bug is real and small if someone wants it: in lib/url.cpp, escape_project_url() takes `char& last = out[strlen(out)-1]` and conditionally writes to it; when escape_url_readable() yields an empty string (e.g. input "http://" or ""), that's out[-1] — an out-of-bounds read, and a write if the stray byte is '_'. A length guard fixes it. Thanks, and sorry for the noise.

Thanks for the pointer. Fixed: the commit message now uses the `Assisted-by:` trailer per the AI assistants usage policy instead of a co-author line.

The VmSwap reading is unchanged, and the `mem_usage` lines agree with
`/proc/pid/status`.

One commit does touch the measurement, though not that part of it. `procinfo_app()`
counts a process twice when an app reports an `<other_pid>` that is also a child of
its main process: `add_child_totals()` walks it, and then the outer loop adds the
same pid again because it never checked `p.scanned`. CPU time, RSS, virtual size
and swap usage all come out doubled for that process. That one stands on its own.

What the PR is about: when a job has no running process there is no `VmSwap` to
read, so `enforce_run_list()` falls back to this:

```cpp
    } else {
        erss = rp->avp->max_rss;
        eswap = rp->avp->max_rss;  // best guess
    }
```

and that is where an RSS figure ends up being compared against swap space. You
asked for `mem_usage_debug`, so here it is on current master: four jobs of one app
version, 800 MB resident each, swap limit 480 MB, and nothing on the host swapping
at all.

```
23:22:02 [mem_usage] test_result_0: virtual size 0.78 GB, RSS 0.78 GB, swap usage 0.00 GB
23:22:02 [mem_usage] test_result_1: virtual size 0.78 GB, RSS 0.78 GB, swap usage 0.00 GB
23:22:02 [mem_usage] BOINC totals: RSS 1.57 GB, swap usage 0.00 GB
23:22:03 [mem_usage] enforce: available RAM 28.15 GB, swap space 0.47 GB
23:22:03 [cpu_sched_debug] skipping test_result_2: swap usage (0.69 GB) exceeds swap left (0.47 GB)
23:22:03 [cpu_sched_debug] skipping test_result_3: swap usage (0.69 GB) exceeds swap left (0.47 GB)
```

The `mem_usage` lines are correct, and that is the point: swap usage really is
0.00 GB. The 0.69 GB the last two jobs are refused on is `rss_smoothed` of the
running job, arriving through `max_rss`; they never start, with a CPU free the
whole time. That is what #7132 and #7146 look like from the user's side.

Tracking `APP_VERSION::max_swap_usage` next to `max_rss`, by the same rule, covers
it. When nothing is swapping it is zero, so it imposes no limit at all; swap usage
is a property of memory pressure rather than of the job.

I'm not arguing that a swap-killed job should come back sooner. What I'd like to
separate out is that `swap_limit_check()` returns true and `schedule_cpus()` then
skips the scheduler entirely for that pass:

```cpp
    if (!swap_limit_check()) {
        make_run_list(run_list);
        return enforce_run_list(run_list);
    }
    return true;
```

so the run list becomes whatever `swap_limit_check()` built, and that only ever
contains jobs which are already running or swap-killed. Jobs of a different app,
using no swap at all, are not considered. Two jobs holding 0.39 GB of real
`VmSwap` each against a 0.53 GB limit, plus two jobs of a second app that never
swap:

```
23:23:49 [cpu_sched_debug] swap usage limit exceeded: 0.78 GB > 0.53 GB
23:23:49 [cpu_sched_debug] killing test_result_0
23:23:49 [cpu_sched_debug] scheduling test_result_1
23:23:49 [cpu_sched_debug] skipping test_result_0: swap usage (0.39 GB) exceeds swap left (0.14 GB)
23:23:49 [cpu_sched_debug] using only 1.00 out of 2 CPUs
...
23:23:59 [cpu_sched_debug] checking for runnable swap-killed tasks
23:23:59 [cpu_sched_debug] using only 1.00 out of 2 CPUs
```

The killed job not coming back is the conservatism you describe, and I'll leave it
alone; its `procinfo.swap_usage` is frozen at 0.39 GB because `get_memory_usage()`
skips `PROCESS_UNINITIALIZED` tasks, so the figure can only be an over-estimate.
But `make_run_list()` is not called again either, so the second app never starts
and a CPU sits idle for the rest of the run. I don't think it needs to hold back
jobs that have nothing to do with swap.

With the limit below what one job holds, the kill loop can't stop early, so master
kills that job too:

```
23:24:58 [cpu_sched_debug] swap usage limit exceeded: 0.78 GB > 0.28 GB
23:24:58 [cpu_sched_debug] killing test_result_0
23:24:58 [cpu_sched_debug] killing test_result_1
...
23:25:08 [cpu_sched_debug] checking for runnable swap-killed tasks
23:25:08 [cpu_sched_debug] using only 0.00 out of 2 CPUs
```

After that nothing is executing, and every later pass takes the revive branch,
where each job's frozen figure (0.39 GB) exceeds the whole limit (0.28 GB) and
vetoes everything behind it; `make_run_list()` is never called again. The second
app's jobs were never considered, for the rest of the run.

There is no setting of this that is simply right: the swap usage of a job that
isn't running can't be measured, so you're guessing either way. Comparing RSS
against swap space is the wrong quantity rather than a cautious estimate of the
right one; counting a process twice is wrong at any setting; and stopping
unrelated jobs from being scheduled at all isn't caution about the killed job,
it's collateral (Missile).

`swap_limit_check()` no longer returns anything and no longer builds a run list. It
kills when we're over the limit and revives what fits when we're under it, and
scheduling goes back to `make_run_list()` and `enforce_run_list()`, which already
apply the swap test to each job's own figure. The kill loop skips jobs that hold no
swap, since killing one frees nothing and costs it its checkpoint, and it leaves
the last job that does hold swap running: if we're still over the limit by then,
that job exceeds it alone and killing it brings us nothing. Running one job over
the limit seemed better than running none. (The Android special case from the
earlier version of this branch is gone; it wasn't a proper fix for this.)

One issue I know about. A killed job whose frozen figure lands between what's left
and the whole limit still won't be revived while other jobs are using swap, even
though the dead process holds none. I only zero that figure when it exceeds the
whole limit and the process is gone, because zeroing it unconditionally is the
restart loop you're describing.

The logs come from a "harness" that runs the real client with the scheduler exactly
as built; nothing in it models scheduling. `swap_worker` calls
`madvise(MADV_PAGEOUT)`, so `VmSwap` is a known number and the runs repeat exactly.
It replaces `client/app_test.cpp` and one line of `app_start.cpp`.

https://github.com/KNineLat/boinc-scheduler_star

`./compare.sh --prebuilt` runs both clients over every scenario:

```
                                          master    patched
e1  unstarted jobs charged RSS as swap
    idle CPU passes                         1          0

e2  scheduling after swap kill (real VmSwap)
    jobs killed                             1          1
    make_run_list() after kill              1          6
    idle CPU passes                         5          5

e3  second app (no swap) alongside swap kill
    jobs killed                             1          1
    second app scheduled                    0          5
    idle CPU passes                         5          0

e4  one job exceeds limit alone
    jobs killed                             2          1
    second app scheduled                    0          9
    idle CPU passes                         9          0
```

In e2 the killed job doesn't come back in either build; what changes is that `make_run_list()` runs again, so
other jobs aren't locked out. In e3 and e4 the second app holds zero swap and starts immediately on
the patched build.

I can talk about several exceptions here, however these are exceptions, not a generic trend:

2. We have only 1 project (PrimeGrid) that has Windows on ARM application.

Apple SoC and Windows on ARM are the platforms with good performance, and they give to the Projects a real performance gain.
Docker-based applications are different: they provide scientists a possibility to create a single application that will run on every platform (ok, almost any).

Here I can think about those platforms only that are not powerful enough or have a very exotic OS/architecture where there is not way to install a normal BOINC application.

@AenBleidd Please make sure all parentheses, braces, etc. are fully balanced in each source file, even when ignoring all #if, #ifdef, and other compile conditionals. #ifdef __WXMSW__

 . . .
 pTaskbar->QueueBalloon(
#endif

```
#ifdef __WXMSW__
 . . .
pTaskbar->SetBalloon
#else
 . . .
 pTaskbar->QueueBalloon
#endif
      (

This is likely `send_report_post_email()` (`html/inc/forum_email.inc`) failing at the SMTP level — the "Your report could not be recorded" message is actually the correct, honest failure path in `forum_report_post.php`. The underlying bug is that `send_report_post_email()` is called before any `page_head()` call in this file, so a failed send's raw `echo $mail->ErrorInfo` (from inside `send_email()`, `html/inc/email.inc`) lands before the page's `<head>`/stylesheet output and breaks the page's CSS — which may be what's actually being observed here, on top of (or instead of) a genuine mail delivery problem worth checking on this project's own SMTP config.

Suggested fix for the CSS/ordering half: buffer the send (`ob_start()`/`ob_get_clean()`) and replay the captured output inside whichever of the three `page_head()` branches ends up rendering, since the page title depends on the outcome so a simple reorder isn't enough. Happy to open a PR.

The team_import.php crash here has a specific root cause: handle_team() (called from main()'s per-team loop) has no try/catch around it at all, so any uncaught exception during processing — a duplicate-key collision, an encoding issue like the one in this report, or anything else a single team's data can trigger — kills the entire run mid-list. Every team after the failing one silently never gets processed, and since most collisions/data issues recur identically on every subsequent run, the import can get stuck at the exact same point forever.

Confirmed this independently via a different trigger: two real official teams whose placeholder founder both had the display name "Coordinador" hit user.name's unique constraint, throwing the same uncaught mysqli_sql_exception shown in this report's own stack trace (just via BoincUser::insert() in make_user() rather than BoincTeam::update()).

Fix: wrap each team's handle_team() call in try/catch so one team's failure becomes an isolated, logged skip instead of a total outage — every other team still gets processed. Tested against a deliberately crafted collision fixture: the unpatched script reproduces the exact crash-and-stop behavior; the patched version logs the failure and continues to the next team.

Happy to open a PR for this fix.

Design proposal. (@rafabelts — you offered to take this a year ago; nothing's happened since, happy to coordinate if you're still keen, otherwise I'll run with it.)

## The problem

`get_path()` keys every entry on `$_SERVER["PHP_SELF"]`'s basename (`get_cached_data`/`set_cached_data` never pass an explicit name). So the page name is acting as an **accidental namespace**, which means:

- **The same data gets cached N times.** `get_other_projects()` (`inc/user.inc`) is called from `show_user.php`, `home.php`, and `cert_all.php` — the identical free-dc.org response for one user is stored under three keys, fetched three times, with no coherent way to invalidate.
- **Invalidation is by hard-coded literal.** `create_profile.php:351` does `clear_cache_entry("view_profile.php", "userid=$user->id")` — it works today only because `"view_profile.php"` and its `$cache_args` format are duplicated in two files with nothing keeping them in sync. And it *doesn't* clear `show_user.php`'s entry, which caches the same profile data under `USER_PAGE_TTL` — so `show_user.php` serves a stale profile/community-links block for up to an hour after an edit.
- **Two pages can't share an entry**, and there's an asymmetry: `clear_cache_entry` takes an explicit page name, `get`/`set` don't.

## Minimal fix (what the issue asks for)

Replace the PHP_SELF key with a required, caller-supplied data name:

```php
get_cached_data($max_age, $name, $params)
set_cached_data($max_age, $name, $data, $params)
clear_cache_entry($name, $params)
```

- **All parameters required, no defaults** — so every un-migrated call site (all 22) fails immediately with `ArgumentCountError` at a known line, rather than silently mis-binding (`set_cached_data($ttl, serialize($x), $args)` would otherwise write the args string as the payload). One commit, hard break — the API is internal, no external consumers.
- On-disk name becomes `cache/<xx>/<name>[_<params>]`.
- **`$name` must be unique per call site and describe the stored structure — never derived from `$params`.** Today PHP_SELF is the *only* thing separating `top_hosts.php` / `top_users.php` / `top_teams.php` (byte-identical `$cache_args`), `view_profile.php` / `show_user.php` (both `userid=N`, different object shapes), and `team_display.php` / `team_members.php` (both `teamid=N`, decorated record vs bare record). A careless `$name` there → `unserialize()` succeeds, wrong object, broken page, no error.
- Put the `$name` + TTL pairs in `cache_parameters.inc` as constants (also kills the ad-hoc `CACHE_PERIOD` / bare `3600` literals). I'll bring a per-call-site name table with the PR.
- Callers that already pass a type string (`"job_status"`, `"os"`, `"project_config_platform_xml"`) just move it to the `$name` slot.

Migration: on deploy every existing entry orphans — file entries reaped by mtime (≤7 d), memcache by TTL (≤1 d); brief DB-load bump, self-heals. Bump `MEMCACHE_PREFIX` / clear `../cache/` for an instant cutover.

## Or the actual rewrite

A small `Cache` class — `Cache::get($name, $params, $max_age)` / `::set` / `::clear` — with the file/memcache split behind one interface, a single `key()` method (one place to sanitize + hash overlong keys, replacing the five scattered `strstr($x, "..")` guards), and a consistent `null`-on-miss. Same call-site churn as the rename, addresses more of "poorly designed." Your call which way to go.

## Smaller things noticed, worth folding in either way

- **Delete `start_cache()` / `end_cache()`** — marked DEPRECATED, one caller (`ops/eah_server_status.php`, which passes mismatched TTLs `1800`→`600`), and their memcache branch is a PHP 8 fatal (`$cache->timestamp` on an array). Port that page to `get`/`set_cached_data`.
- **Drop `$no_cache` and the `apache_request_headers()` call at `cache.inc:130`** — the result is assigned and never used (dead since the If-Modified-Since removal); `$no_cache` currently just disables caching under CLI.
- **Normalize miss → `null`.** The memcache branch returns `false` on a miss; cf. the guards added in #7307 against `unserialize(false)`.
- **Atomic writes** — `set_cached_data`'s file branch is `fopen/fwrite/fclose`; a concurrent reader can `unserialize()` a half-written file. Temp file + `rename()`.
- `substr(md5(...), 1, 2)` → offset 0 while in there.

Two independent standalone bugs from the same read are filed separately: #7317 (`USER_HOST_TTL` undefined → PHP 8 fatal in `cache_check_diskspace()`) and #7318 (`BoincMemcache::get()` rebuilds the connection + re-adds servers every call).

BoincBatchFileAssoc::delete_aux("job_file_id=$file->id");
```

`BoincBatchFileAssoc` (`html/inc/submit_db.inc:142`) defines only `insert()`, `lookup()`, an instance `delete()`, and `delete_batch()` — there is no static `delete_aux()` and no `__callStatic`. (`delete_aux()` is a method on the `BoincDb` connection object, which the class's own `delete()`/`delete_batch()` call as `$db->delete_aux(...)`; it was never a class-level method.) So this line is a fatal `Call to undefined method BoincBatchFileAssoc::delete_aux()`.

It's reached only after `unlink($path)` and the `echo "deleted $path\n"` on the two preceding lines, and it precedes `$file->delete()`. So even where the daemon does run (a project that installed `schema_condor.sql` and scheduled it), each pass: unlinks the download file, prints "deleted", then fatals before removing the `job_file` row. On restart `$id` is back to 0, the same now-file-less row is re-selected, and it fatals again on the same line — the daemon can never remove a `job_file` DB row or make progress past the first eligible one.

Present since the 2017 "fix delete_job_files" (#1844 / `b68e0dafa`), which introduced the `_mysql_fetch_object` refactor but left this call. Combined with the inverted condition above, the daemon deletes in-use files from disk and then immediately crashes without cleaning up the DB.

Fix: replace with a real deletion — either add a `BoincBatchFileAssoc` class method for "delete all rows for a `job_file_id`" (mirroring `delete_batch()`), or inline the query via `BoincDb::get()->delete_aux('batch_file_assoc', "job_file_id=$file->id")`.

## Current state

The `job_file` / `batch_file_assoc` / `delete_job_files` triad already sketches this feature; the gaps below are what stop it working, and v1 is mostly finishing and wiring it in.

**1. `sched/file_deleter.cpp` deletes a shared input as soon as the first WU using it is assimilated and its results validated.**
`wu_delete_files()` unlinks every `<file_info>` in `wu.xml_doc` that lacks `<no_delete/>` (or a WU name containing `"nodelete"`). `transitioner.cpp:549-554` sets `file_delete_state = FILE_DELETE_READY` **per WU**, from that WU's own results — there is no refcount across WUs that share a physical download file. So a 1 GB `jf_<md5>` used by 1000 WUs is `unlink`ed from `download/` when WU #1 is assimilated, and WUs #2-1000 404. `<sticky/>` is a client-only flag (`file_deleter` never reads it; the client parses and discards `<no_delete/>`), so `<sticky/>` and `<no_delete/>` are independent axes, and the server side has no per-file lifetime logic beyond `<no_delete/>` (and the `nodelete`-in-WU-name shortcut). The issue text itself states the gap: "Currently we can make the file sticky. That does 1) but not 2)."

**2. `batch_file_assoc` isn't part of a normal project.**
It's defined only in `db/schema_condor.sql`; `py/Boinc/database.py::create_database()` runs only `schema.sql` / `constraints.sql` / `content.sql`, and no `db_update.php` migration creates it. On a normal project the table is absent, and the write path doesn't degrade: on pre-8.1 PHP `BoincBatchFileAssoc::insert()` returns false and the association is silently lost; on PHP 8.1+ (mysqli exceptions on by default, never turned off) it throws an uncaught `mysqli_sql_exception` out of `db_conn.inc`'s `do_query()` and 500s the RPC — the same failure mode documented in #4779's stack trace. Reachable without the condor schema: the access gate is a `user_submit` row, which is in base `schema.sql`.

**3. Almost nothing populates `job_file` / `batch_file_assoc`.**
The only writer is `job_file.php`'s remote-file-management RPCs (`query_files` / `upload_files`). `submit_rpc_handler.php::stage_file()` — the staging path for the remote batch-submission RPC (`submit_api.py` / `boinc_submit`) — copies files into `download/` (as `jf_<md5>` for the content-addressed modes) and creates no row. (BUDA's staging path also creates no rows — see decision 3.) `upload_files()` inserts `job_file` without a `lookup_name()` first, so on an upgraded (non-unique-index) project it can create duplicate `name` rows.

**4. `html/ops/delete_job_files` is currently non-functional and unscheduled (tracked in #7319).**
Its first DB call — `BoincJobFile::enum()` at line 34 — is an undefined-method fatal (`BoincJobFile` in `submit_db.inc` defines only `insert` / `lookup_name` / `delete` / `update`, with no parent class), so the script aborts on its first loop iteration, before touching disk or the DB. Past that, more is wrong: the row set is gated on a client-supplied `delete_time` (set via `job_file.php`'s `query_files` / `upload_files`); the active-batch check is inverted (`if (!$b) continue;` would delete the file exactly when a running batch still needs it, and never reap one whose batches are all done); it `unlink`s only `$path`, orphaning the `$path.md5` sidecar; and `BoincBatchFileAssoc::delete_aux()` (line 53, before `$file->delete()`) is undefined too (`delete_aux()` is a two-arg `DbConn` instance method). It's scheduled nowhere (no `config.xml` `<task>`). Filed as #7319; this feature needs it repaired and running.

**5. `job_file.name` uniqueness diverges by install age.**
Fresh installs get `UNIQUE jf_name(name)` from `constraints.sql`; upgraded installs have a non-unique index (still literally named `md5` — the 2017 migration renamed the column but not the index, and nothing re-runs `constraints.sql`).

## Proposed v1 — shared input survives while its batches need it (no client-facing surface, no "pinned")

1. **Schema.** Move `batch_file_assoc` into `schema.sql`, and add a `db_update.php` function for existing projects that, in order: creates `batch_file_assoc` (`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` — Condor projects that ran `schema_condor.sql` already have it); collapses duplicate `job_file.name` rows (item 5) keeping `MIN(id)`, repoints the `job_file_id` in any `batch_file_assoc` rows that referenced the losers, and drops the `(job_file_id, batch_id)` duplicates that repoint can create (`batch_file_assoc` has no declared foreign key — it's a logical reference, with a `(job_file_id, batch_id)` unique key); then adds the `jf_name` unique key. That collapse deletes rows, so it should log every one and, if you'd rather `db_update.php` not mutate data silently, be split out as its own clearly-labelled step a project runs deliberately. `workunit(batch)` is already indexed everywhere (`wu_batch` from `constraints.sql` / `db_update.php::update_2_15_2025`), so nothing to add there — the reaper's join is already covered.

2. **Populate the tables on the remote-submission staging path.**
   - `stage_file()` (non-`remote` modes) → create one `job_file` row per unique staged physical name. `job_file` has only `(id, name, create_time, delete_time)` — no md5, size or owner column — so the row carries only the staged physical name (plus timestamps). Of the non-`remote` modes, `local` / `semilocal` / `inline` return a `jf_<md5>` name and `sandbox` is meant to (it currently reaches its name only via the fall-through bug below); `local_staged` returns the submitter's own filename. Set `delete_time = 0` on these rows and let the batch-state interlock (item 4) govern lifetime — but the existing `job_file.php` callers *do* set a meaningful `delete_time`, so how the interlock treats it is decision 8.
   - `batch_file_assoc` rows → a **new pass in `submit_batch()` after the batch row exists**. `stage_files()` runs at `submit_rpc_handler.php:479`, before the `BoincBatch::insert()` at `:529` (the add-to-existing-batch path has a `batch_id` sooner but doesn't thread it into staging either), so `stage_file()` has no batch to reference. The new pass walks the batch's unique input names → `BoincJobFile::lookup_name()` → insert `(batch_id, job_file_id)`, tolerating the `(job_file_id, batch_id)` unique-key dup (one file used by N jobs in a batch → one assoc row).
   - Every `job_file` / `batch_file_assoc` insert is dup-key-tolerant (check return *and* catch — pre-8.1 returns false, 8.1+ throws).
   - Fix `submit_rpc_handler.php:187` `case 'sandbox':` while here — it has no `break`/`return` and falls through into `case "inline":`, which md5s the sandbox link *name* and writes that string as the file contents. One-line fix (`return $phys_name;`).
   - `remote` mode stays out — a genuinely remote file has no copy in `download/`, nothing to track.

3. **`file_deleter.cpp::wu_delete_files()` skips any input that has a `job_file` row.** A tracked job file's lifetime belongs to the reaper (item 4), not the per-WU transitioner path. The skip returns success, so the WU still advances to `FILE_DELETE_DONE` with the file left on disk. There's no C++ `job_file` class today; `file_deleter` already links `boinc_db`, so this is a raw `do_query` or a small `DB_JOB_FILE`.
   **Items 3 and 4 need to land together** — item 3 alone would trade the 404 for a permanent disk leak. Behaviour change to note: after this, *all* remote-submission input files (shared or single-use) wait for batch completion + the reaper instead of per-WU deletion. If that's too broad a default, the skip can sit behind a config flag (on for projects that use remote submission) — see decision 2.

4. **Fix and schedule `delete_job_files`.** The bug-fixes (give `BoincJobFile` an `enum()` — or rewrite line 34 as a raw query — so the script runs at all; invert the check; replace the dead `BoincBatchFileAssoc::delete_aux(...)` call with a real deletion — either `$db->delete_aux('batch_file_assoc', "job_file_id=$id")` on a `BoincDb::get()` handle, or a new `BoincBatchFileAssoc::delete_by_job_file()` static mirroring the existing `delete_batch()`; `unlink` the `.md5` too; replace the hardcoded `dir_hier_path($file->name, "../../download", $fanout)` with `download_hier_path($file->name)`, which reads `download_dir` from config) can land via #7319. On top of that, item 4 adds the interlock this feature needs: delete a `job_file` (physical file + `.md5` + rows) only when, for every batch it's associated with, `batch.state >= COMPLETE` **and** every workunit in that batch is at `file_delete_state = FILE_DELETE_DONE` — the same signal `file_deleter` gates on (indexed via `wu_filedel`). (All WUs in the batch, not just those referencing this file — simpler, an indexed query, at the cost of holding the file a little longer. A `job_file` with no `batch_file_assoc` rows at all — staging succeeded, batch creation didn't — passes this vacuously and is reaped next pass; harmless, a resubmit re-stages.) Whether it also keeps the client-supplied `delete_time` floor (`job_file.php`'s callers set one) is decision 8. It covers RETIRED batches with still-running sent WUs: `retire_batch()` only cancels *unsent* WUs, and `sched_resend.cpp` re-dispatches without checking the file exists. Schedule it as a `<task>` in the sample `config.xml`.

The intent of v1: a shared input would survive all its WUs and be deleted from `download/` when every batch that used it is finished — no pin flag, no scheduler change, no client-visible surface. One limitation to be explicit about: v1 fixes only the server side. A submitter who also wants to skip client re-downloads still has to put `<sticky/>` in their own input template, and once they do, v1 gives no automatic un-stick path — the client keeps that file until `sticky_expire_time` (unset by default) or a manual reset. Blanket client cleanup only arrives with v2's scheduler pass.

## Proposed v2 — the "pinned" concept from the issue body

To keep a file on clients and server *past* the lifetime of the batch that last used it. Two concrete pieces, then a fork the rest hangs off.

**Concrete:**

- **`job_file.pinned TINYINT`** (default 0; standard BOINC boolean column). Read by two things: `delete_job_files` (don't reap even when all batches are done) and the scheduler pass below. `file_deleter` never checks it — item 3 already makes it skip every tracked file. Note: on the content-addressed `stage_file()` modes (`local` / `semilocal` / `inline`, and `sandbox` once its fall-through bug is fixed) the physical name is `jf_<md5>`, so two submitters with the same content share one `job_file` row and one `pinned` bit — "pinned" means "someone pinned it". (`local_staged` keeps the submitter's own filename, so identical content staged that way gets separate rows.)

- **A scheduler pass** in `sched_files.cpp` (new config flag; hard-off under locality scheduling; `sched_files.cpp` gains a DB dependency it doesn't have today). It runs **right after `open_database()` in `handle_request.cpp`** (~line 1290) — after `do_file_delete_regex()`, past the two DB-free early returns; *not* near `send_file_deletes()`, which is a locality-only function outside `process_request()`. For each `<file_info>` the client reports (a stock non-locality client reports only its sticky files), it looks up the `job_file` row and, if the file is unpinned and its "still needed?" predicate is false — **the same predicate the item-4 reaper uses**: no association to a batch with `state < COMPLETE`, *and* every WU in those batches at `file_delete_state = FILE_DELETE_DONE` — adds `<delete_file_info>`. Sharing the reaper's exact predicate avoids a client dropping a file and then re-downloading 1 GB on a resend. The pass must also be able to *remove* a pinned name that `do_file_delete_regex()` queued (or the comment documents "incompatible with a `jf_*`-matching `file_delete_regex`"). Placement consequence: unpin rides on normal scheduler traffic — it propagates on any RPC that gets past the two pre-DB early returns (essentially every real report-or-request contact; the exceptions are a wrong client version / `dont_send_jobs` with nothing reported, and the `nowork_skip` hack). The project can't push an unpin out of band.

**The fork — where "pinned" lives.** "Pinned" is naturally a per-user sandbox-file property, but the deleters read `job_file.pinned` from the DB, and nothing in the DB tracks sandbox files today (`sandbox.php` / `sandbox.inc` are filesystem-only: `<project>/sandbox/<userid>/<name>` + a `.md5/<name>` sidecar). All three options add DB-backing there:

- **A — a `.pinned` marker file mirrored to `job_file.pinned`.** Smallest, matches the `.md5`-sidecar pattern; but one shared `pinned` bit per content hash (unpin clears it for everyone) and no home for the reminder-email owner.
- **B — a `user_file` table, `job_file.pinned` derived from it.** Fixes the shared-bit and email-owner problems and allows pinning before first submission; costs a new table + migration + DB-backing the sandbox pages.
- **C — pin on `job_file` only, sandbox page toggles it.** Least schema change; but no row exists until first submission, and still one shared bit per hash.

Whichever option: `sandbox.php::delete_file()` (today a bare `unlink` of the sandbox copy + its `.md5` sidecar, no DB check) would refuse on a file whose `job_file` row has an association to a non-RETIRED batch. Rationale is **pin integrity** (don't orphan a `pinned=1` row by removing the source that backs it), not job safety - deleting the sandbox copy doesn't touch the `download/` copy a running job uses. Open question: can a file be unpinned while still in a non-retired batch? (See decision 5.)

**Client re-download (`<sticky/>`).** Server retention is already handled by item 3's DB check, so this is client-side only. Two approaches:
- *targeted inject* - add a field to `INFILE_DESC`, a `create_work` arg, thread `job_file.pinned` through `submit_jobs()`, have `process_input_template.cpp` emit `<sticky/>` for the pinned file's `<file_info>` (chain across PHP->C++, ~4-5 files);
- *blanket* - every tracked input gets `<sticky/>`; the scheduler pass un-sticks the unpinned ones once done. Simpler, but it re-introduces the blanket `<sticky/>` that `debc363410` took out of BUDA's generated templates. If that was dropped because nothing un-stuck the files, does the scheduler pass providing that path change the call?

**Later (not v2 core): reminder emails + auto-unpin.** A cron task nags owners of pinned-but-idle files to unpin (optional auto-unpin after N days). Owner identification is clean under B, fuzzy otherwise; `sent_email` (PK `userid`) would need a per-file `last_reminded`.

`db_purge` needs no changes - it purges `workunit`/`result` rows already at `FILE_DELETE_DONE` and never touches `job_file` rows or `download/` files.

## Decisions I'd want from you

1. **Existing work?** Given the adjacent work noted above, is there a branch/direction I should build against rather than starting cold?

2. **Phasing.** Land it as v1 (plumbing + reaper; no pin, no client surface) then v2 (pin flag + scheduler pass), reminder emails / auto-unpin later - OK? And OK with item 3's behaviour change (after v1, *every* `job_file`-tracked input waits for the reaper, not just shared ones), or should that skip be config-gated?

3. **Is BUDA in scope?** Its batch inputs already carry `<no_delete/>` (so problem #1 doesn't touch it) and use per-batch names (`batch_<id>_<md5>`, no cross-batch dedup), staged from the batch ZIP not the sandbox - so the sandbox-based pin mechanism can't reach them. Give BUDA `job_file` rows under its existing names (reaper coverage only, no rename), or defer entirely?

4. **Where does "pinned" live** - (A) a `.pinned` marker file mirrored to `job_file.pinned`; (B) a new `user_file` DB table with `job_file.pinned` derived from it; or (C) `job_file.pinned` only, with the sandbox page as the UI? No DB table tracks sandbox files today, so all three make sandbox file-management DB-backed. A leaves one shared `pinned` bit per content hash and no home for email ownership; B fixes both but is the biggest lift; C can't pin before first submission. The client-`<sticky/>` and reminder-email pieces both depend on this choice.

5. **Can a file be unpinned while it's still in a non-retired batch?** The issue body says a pinned file "can't be changed or deleted while it's associated with a non-retired batch" but is silent on unpin. Two readings: (a) unpin allowed anytime, with the resulting deletion still batch-state-gated; (b) unpin blocked until the batch retires, mirroring the change/delete restriction. This shapes the scheduler pass and the reminder flow.

6. **`<sticky/>` for pinned inputs** - targeted inject vs blanket (see v2 → *Client re-download*) - which way?

7. **The `delete_job_files` repair** (the `enum()` fatal, the inverted check, the undefined `delete_aux`, the orphaned `.md5`, `download_hier_path()`, plus the one-line `case 'sandbox':` fall-through in `submit_rpc_handler.php`) - land standalone in #7319, or in this work? The `file_delete_state` interlock on top is feature-coupled (needs items 2+3), but the defect repair can go first either way.

8. **`delete_time` semantics.** `job_file.php`'s header (`:40-43`) and `delete_job_files` both document the reaper's gate as "the delete date is in the past **and** there are no associations to active batches" — a client-supplied `delete_time` floor ANDed with a batch check. v1.4 keeps that AND but redefines the batch half (batch state + per-WU `FILE_DELETE_DONE`). Keep the client `delete_time` floor as well, or drop it and let batch state be the whole story? The new staging path (item 2) sets `delete_time = 0`, so this only affects the existing `job_file.php` callers.

9. **Reap at `COMPLETE` or `RETIRED`?** `delete_job_files`'s comment says "retired batches" but its code tests `state < COMPLETE`; v1.4 and the v2 pass follow the code (`state >= COMPLETE` + every WU at `FILE_DELETE_DONE`). Keep that, or wait for `RETIRED`? `COMPLETE` reclaims disk sooner; `RETIRED` keeps a shared input available for a resubmit against a batch whose jobs have finished but that the submitter hasn't closed out. The per-WU `FILE_DELETE_DONE` check is a safety net either way.

Hello, I am a user of both BOINC and openSUSE so I'm interested in fixing this issue.
I have reproduced this and would like to take it, if that's alright.

**Reproduced** with the official `boinc-client-8.2.15-4612.x86_64_suse16_0.rpm`
in an openSUSE Leap 16.0 container running systemd as PID 1: `%post` fails with
`Failed to execute /usr/lib/systemd/systemd-sysv-install`, zypper returns 107,
and the service is left `disabled`.

**Root cause** (confirmed): the RPM ships `/etc/init.d/boinc-client` alongside
the native unit. Because an init script matching the unit name is present,
`systemctl enable` tries to sync SysV state via `systemd-sysv-install`, which
Leap 16 no longer provides, so the whole enable aborts.

**Scope**: `suse16_0` is the only openSUSE RPM the workflow builds, so in practice
this is a Leap 16.0 issue — which matches your report. The trigger is general
(`systemctl enable` aborts on any systemd host where `systemd-sysv-install` is
absent), and 16.0 is where that helper is gone from the distribution entirely:
openSUSE dropped the `systemd-sysvcompat` package that used to provide it, so a
stock 16.0 install hits this every time.
- Not affected: Fedora (its systemctl doesn't synchronize SysV state, so it never
  calls the helper) and the `.deb` (Debian/Ubuntu still provide the helper, so
  `systemctl enable` succeeds) — both verified. The `.deb` also packages the init
  script but enables fine, so I'd leave it untouched.

**On the fix:** your suggested fix — not shipping the SysV script on these
systemd-only targets, is exactly right, and I agree the alternative you flag
(making `%post` tolerate the sync failure) isn't the real fix: it would hide the
install-time error but leave every later `systemctl enable`/`disable` cycle
broken. So part one is simply to stop shipping the script in the RPM packages.

**One thing to add beyond that:** the upgrade path. On a fresh install, not
shipping the script is sufficient. But upgrading *from* an already-affected
package still fails, because RPM runs the new `%post` before it removes the old
package's files — so the old init script is still on disk during `%post` and
re-triggers the sync. Moving the client's `systemctl enable --now` from `%post`
to `%posttrans` (which runs after the old files are gone) covers that case. I
only noticed it when testing the upgrade, so flagging it explicitly.

One consequence worth noting: `tests/linux_package_integration_tests.py` asserts
`/etc/init.d/boinc-client` exists and is root-owned, and it runs against both the
`.deb` and the RPM jobs. Since the script now ships only on `.deb`, I made those
two assertions conditional on `dpkg` so they still run for `.deb` and are skipped
for the RPM targets — otherwise `test-fedora-rpm-package` / `test-opensuse-rpm-package`
would fail.

I've implemented both parts and tested fresh install, upgrade, workaround-then-
upgrade, and uninstall on Leap 16, plus fresh install and upgrade on Fedora 43.
**Most relevant to the reported symptom:** after restarting the container (systemd
re-init, which re-evaluates enabled units), the stock package leaves the client
dead (inactive, no process), while the fixed package auto-starts it and it
responds to `boinccmd` — i.e. it now survives the reboot that the report calls
out. Happy to open a PR if the approach looks right.

I can confirm the premise empirically, and trace the consequence through to a user-visible behaviour. I have no BOINC installed on the machine below, which makes it a clean measurement: **every CPU-second `vmmem` accumulates here is non-BOINC work.**

## Measured

Windows 11, 16 logical CPUs, a WSL2 distro running an unrelated workload (a blockchain node), no BOINC anywhere on the system:

```
vmmemWSL CPU in 60s : 60.2 cpu-seconds
equivalent to       : 1.00 fully-busy cores
```

Under heavier WSL use on the same box that figure reaches ~11 cores. All of it would currently be booked as BOINC-related.

Incidentally, `Get-Process | TotalProcessorTime` returns empty for `vmmemWSL`; `Win32_Process` `KernelModeTime + UserModeTime` works. Worth knowing if anyone tries to reproduce this from PowerShell.

## The path through the code

`lib/procinfo.cpp:223`

```cpp
#ifdef _WIN32
    } else if (strstr(p.command, "vmmem")) {
        docker += (p.user_time + p.kernel_time);
#endif
```

`strstr` matches **`vmmemWSL`**, not just `vmmem`, so this catches the WSL2 VM process on current Windows builds. The whole VM's CPU time is added.

From there:

```
lib/procinfo.cpp:232     brc = boinc_app + low_prio + vbox + docker
client/app.cpp:600       nbrc = total_cpu_time_now - brc
client/app.cpp:612       non_boinc_cpu_usage = delta_nbrc / (delta_t * p_ncpus)
client/cs_prefs.cpp:272  if (non_boinc_cpu_usage*100 > current_suspend_cpu_usage())
```

So inflating `brc` **under-estimates** `non_boinc_cpu_usage`, and the last line is the "suspend when non-BOINC CPU usage exceeds X%" preference. The practical effect is that BOINC keeps computing while the machine is in fact busy — precisely when the user asked it to back off. A WSL-heavy user gets the opposite of the configured behaviour, and nothing in the UI would explain why.

## On the proposed fix

The approach suggested in this issue is already implemented for Linux in the same code path, which seems like a good sign for porting it:

```cpp
// client/app.cpp:583-590  (Linux only today)
for (ACTIVE_TASK* atp: active_tasks) {
    if (atp->app_version->is_docker_app) {
        docker_time += atp->current_cpu_time;
    }
}
brc += docker_time;
```

The comment at `lib/procinfo.cpp:173-177` already spells out the reasoning for doing it that way on Linux.

One thing that may matter when porting: the Linux path sums only `is_docker_app` tasks, but on Windows the WSL VM also backs `wsl_wrapper` jobs. If those are not `is_docker_app`, a straight port would swing the error the other way and start counting genuine BOINC WSL work as non-BOINC.

**What I could not test:** the "need to verify that this is accurate" part. Docker Desktop is installed here but WSL integration is disabled for this distro, so I could not compare a container's reported CPU time against actual consumption. Happy to run that comparison if someone wants it, though it needs a BOINC install to be a fair test of the real path rather than a synthetic one.

### Results: RR simulation fix (`boinc-rrsim-mc-holdback.patch`)

Tested on top of the per-app `mc_max_could_use` patch, with the `last_mc_limit_reltime` check in `compute_rsc_project_reason()` **left as in stock**. BOINC 8.2.13, Linux x86_64. Running on two hosts (128 threads, 125 usable) since 20 Nov.

**Change**

In `RR_SIM::pick_jobs_to_run()`:
- A job that would go over its app's `max_concurrent` (`CONCURRENT_LIMIT_APP`) is skipped. The project stays in the simulation, so its other apps keep being simulated. Before, the code set `at_max_concurrent_limit` and removed the whole project from the rest of that pass.
- `last_mc_limit_reltime` is now set only when a job is **actually held back** by its app's cap, not when an app simply reaches its cap.
- `CONCURRENT_LIMIT_PROJECT` is unchanged.

So the existing check now blocks only while jobs of a capped app are still waiting to start at the end of the buffer.

**Setup**

LHC@home. app_config: ATLAS `max_concurrent` 31 (3 threads), CMS 8 (4 threads), Theory no limit. Buffer 0.25 + 0.03 days = 24,192 s. The server limits each host to 40 ATLAS and 10 Theory, and currently has no CMS limit.

**Results**

1. **Fetching no longer blocked by a cap that's merely reached.** With CMS at 8 running, the client fetches when the buffer runs low. With stock 8.2.13 and the same config, it logged `don't need (CPU: max concurrent job limit)` while cores sat idle.

2. **The brake still works.** Straight after a fetch that queued more CMS, the work-fetch log showed `last MC limit time 27399 total buf 24192`, followed by `Not requesting tasks: don't need (CPU: max concurrent job limit)`. Once CMS tasks finished and the backlog was shorter than the buffer, `last MC limit time` dropped to about 7,270, and normal buffer logic took over again. Queued CMS stayed between 2 and 6 the whole time, compared with about 196 when the check was relaxed without the simulation fix.

3. **The shortfall goes down as tasks arrive.** Overnight sequence:

   | Time | MC shortfall (s) | Result |
   |---|---|---|
   | 03:10 | 1,619,288 | got 11 |
   | 06:19:43 | 2,127,307 | got 9 |
   | 06:19:57 | 1,590,716 | got 7 |
   | 06:20:08 | 1,173,387 | got 5 |
   | 06:20:19 | 875,381 | got 4 |
   | 06:20:30 | 637,040 | got 3 |
   | 06:20:42 | 528,771 | got 4, then fetching stopped |

   Each new job now counts as future work in the simulation, so each request is smaller than the last until the buffer is filled. Without the fix, the shortfall stayed at about 2.2M on every request.

4. **The shortfall matches real idle time.** One sample of 1.41M s matched the queue. 26 of the 31 running ATLAS jobs had 1.8–2.5 h left, and only 9 ATLAS were queued, the server's limit of 40. That leaves about 51 threads idle from about 2.5 h to the end of the buffer at 6.7 h. Adding the rest of the idle time came to about 1.2–1.4M s.

5. **Stable:** no client crashes and no task errors overnight. The host stayed full: 30–31 ATLAS, 7–8 CMS (limited by threads when Theory jobs are running) and 2–4 Theory.

**Observations**

- A request made during the client's `start_delay`, while running jobs are still suspended, is oversized, because the simulation sees no jobs running. That's not caused by this change.
- A host with an AMD GPU and "Use AMD GPU" enabled for the project kept fetching on stock 8.2.13. The GPU resource, which has no cap and no apps, triggered scheduler requests, and CPU work was added to them. That hides the bug on some hosts, so the stall can be harder to reproduce.

**Combined patch** against 8.2.13 (per-app `mc_max_could_use` plus this change): `boinc-mc-fix-combined-v2.patch`.

As noted before, `pick_jobs_to_run()` is also used by the CPU-scheduling simulation that looks for deadline misses. The change should make that more accurate, but someone who knows that code should review it.

I have a proposed fix and would welcome design feedback before it's marked ready for review. There are two small changes in the client:

work_fetch.cpp: mc_max_could_use is estimated per app (each limited app contributes max_concurrent × its largest CPU usage, unlimited apps count all instances, and project_max_concurrent still caps the total), instead of the smallest limit × the largest task usage.
rr_sim.cpp: when one app reaches its max_concurrent, the RR simulation skips that app's remaining jobs but keeps simulating the project's other apps, instead of dropping the whole project. This keeps last_mc_limit_reltime meaningful, so the existing RSC_REASON_MAX_CONCURRENT gate is unchanged.

Nothing changes when no limits are set: in the client simulator, stock and patched give identical results. With ATLAS 31 / CMS 8 on a 128-thread host, the patched client keeps fetching and gives +14% over 30 simulated days. It has also been running on 5 LHC@home hosts since 20 Nov (8.2.13 and 8.2.15).
